answer_text:
Let \(\phi(t)\) be the characteristic function of \(X\) (and of \(Y\), since \(X\) and \(Y\) are i.i.d.):

\[
\phi(t)=\mathbb{E}\big[e^{itX}\big].
\]

Since \(P(X+Y=0)=1\), we have \(X+Y=0\) almost surely, so for every real \(t\),

\[
e^{it(X+Y)}=1
\]

almost surely. Taking expectations gives

\[
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{it(X+Y)}\right]=1.
\]

By independence,

\[
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{it(X+Y)}\right]
=
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{itX}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[e^{itY}\right]
=
\phi(t)^2.
\]

Thus

\[
\phi(t)^2=1
\]

for every \(t\). Since a characteristic function is continuous and \(\phi(0)=1\), we must have

\[
\phi(t)=1
\]

for all \(t\). The characteristic function identically equal to \(1\) corresponds to the degenerate random variable equal to \(0\) almost surely. Therefore,

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
